title: Google swaps Gemini Notebook's fixed daily caps for a compute budget
subtitle: The new model prices each action by prompt complexity, source count, and feature — refreshing every five hours until a weekly ceiling.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google on September 2 replaced Gemini Notebook's per-feature daily caps with a compute-based usage budget. Under the new system, a user's ceiling reflects how much compute their prompts actually cost: prompt complexity, chat length, number of sources loaded into the notebook, and the features being exercised — a short factual query costs the budget far less than generating a multi-source Video Overview or a full Slide Deck. Quotas refresh every five hours until a weekly cap is reached, and a live usage indicator sits directly below the chat window so users can see how much of their current window is spent.

The mechanism matters because it aligns what a user pays for with what a request actually costs to run. Fixed daily caps were easy to reason about but rewarded cheap-and-frequent use over occasional-and-heavy use, which is the opposite of the pattern Google's most engaged Notebook users have. Compute-based limits also let Google suggest alternative outputs when a request would blow the budget — a Slide Deck downgraded to a text summary, for instance — rather than simply blocking the action.

This is the second Google surface to move to the compute-based model, after the main Gemini app earlier in the year. It matches how the underlying infrastructure has always been billed on the developer side, and it mirrors the shift OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft have all been making toward metering on tokens or compute rather than on feature-flag counts. Expect the rest of the consumer AI product surface to follow: as models get cheaper on average and more expensive at the tail, a single daily cap becomes the wrong shape for the workload.

Takeaway for learners: when you use an AI product, notice how it meters you. Feature caps, message caps, token caps, and compute caps each shape what work is worth doing inside the tool. A compute budget rewards learning what your prompts cost — the same question, phrased two ways or attached to two vs. six sources, can spend very different amounts of the same allowance, and paying attention to that pattern is a cheap way to get more out of the same subscription.
